Two indexes are declared in this document's metadata. Every mark below either
names one of them or files in the first, and every judgement this extension
makes about a mark — which entry it indexes, which target it resolves against,
which sort key it files under, which range it pairs with — is made inside the
one index the mark belongs to.

A mark that names no index files in the first declared one:
[Aardvark]{.index}. A mark that names the second files there:
[Babbage]{.index index="authors"}.

A sort key is written for one index and not for the other. The Hague files
under Z in the first, where a mark writes one: [Hague]{.index sort="Zebra"}.
The same term files under H in the second, where no mark writes one:
[Hague]{.index index="authors"}.

A cross-reference resolves inside its own index. This target names a term the
first index carries: [near]{.index entry="Neighbour" see="Aardvark"}. This one
names the same term from the second index, which does not carry it:
[far]{.index index="authors" entry="Stranger" see="Aardvark"}.

A range does not pair across two indexes. This opening is in the first index:
[Cantor]{.index range="open"}, and this closing is in the second:
[Cantor]{.index index="authors" range="close"}. Neither has a counterpart
inside its own index, so each indexes as an ordinary page number.

## A second marker for the first index {#site-again}

The marker below names no index, so it is a second marker for the first one.
The first marker naming an index is the one that places it, so this marker
places nothing and the extension says so.

::: {.qi-index-here}
:::
